To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fatty acid metabolism is altered in asthma, and that this is associated with reduced stearoylation‐coenzyme A desaturase activity and increased levels of pro‐inflammatory lipid mediators.

(i) asthma is associated with a distinct pattern of fatty acid metabolism, (ii) the fatty acid desaturase 1 (FADS1) gene is a susceptibility gene for asthma, and (iii) the FADS1 gene regulates the levels of arachidonic acid (AA), a key substrate for the synthesis of lipid mediators, including leukotrienes and prostaglandins.
obese and nonobes asthma patients have altered fatty acid metabolism, and that this altered metabolism contributes to airway hyperreactivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular and genetic mechanisms of asthma.
the role of fatty acids and their metabolism in asthma and allergic disease.
the role of fatty acids in the pathogenesis and treatment of asthma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
asthma is a heterogeneous disease with a complex pathophysiology.
the fatty acid profile is altered in obese asthma patients, which may contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease.

the altered lipid metabolism in obesity and asthma is a consequence of the inflammatory response, and that it is the result of a combination of factors including increased oxidative stress, altered gene expression and epigenetics, and increased adipose tissue inflammation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fatty acid profile is altered in obese asthmatics and in obese mice with allergic airway disease and that these alterations are associated with reduced stearoy‐coenzyme A desaturase (SCD) activity.

the fatty acid composition of asthma patients differs from healthy controls, that these differences are associated with altered stearoyl-CoA desaturase activity, that the fatty acid changes in asthma are associated with altered lipid mediator signaling, and that the altered lipid mediator signaling in asthma may contribute to airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.
the following fatty acids are altered in asthma patients: palmitoleic acid (C16:1n‐7), palmitic acid (C14:0), and oleic acid (C18:1n‐9).
The main takeaway from our work is that
asthma is characterized by altered fatty acid metabolism and that stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) is a key regulator of this process.
asthma is characterized by a distinct pattern of fatty acid levels, including elevated levels of palmitoleate, and a reduced stearoylation‐coenzyme A desaturase 1 activity.
asthma is associated with altered levels of fatty acids and lipid mediator production, which are associated with reduced desaturase activity and increased inflammation.
